chief_complaint: lower back pain that is worse in the morning
hpi_details: 22M presents with 6 months of chronic lower back pain. It is worst when he wakes up, lasting for over an hour, and significantly improves after he works out or plays sports. NSAIDs provide great relief.
ideas: thinks he pulled a muscle lifting weights

core_concepts: Inflammatory back pain typically begins before age 45 and occurs in people of all genders.
Key feature: pain improves with exercise, worsens with rest, severe morning stiffness.
common_misconceptions: Diagnosing mechanical back pain without asking if it improves with rest or exercise.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize uveitis as an extra-articular manifestation (red, painful eye).
management_principles: Obtain SI-joint radiographs; consider MRI if suspicion remains despite non-diagnostic radiographs. HLA-B27 supports but does not establish the diagnosis. Use NSAIDs only after checking renal, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, anticoagulant, and pregnancy considerations; refer to rheumatology for disease-modifying treatment, including biologics when indicated, with infection screening and monitoring.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Clinical Guidance

reference_soap.subjective: 22M with chronic inflammatory low back pain (worse in AM, improves with exercise).
reference_soap.objective: Decreased lumbar flexion (positive Schober test). Tenderness over SI joints.
reference_soap.plan: Obtain SI-joint radiographs and HLA-B27 testing; consider MRI if radiographs are non-diagnostic. Use an NSAID only if appropriate after renal, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, anticoagulant, and pregnancy-risk review. Refer to rheumatology; urgently assess new weakness, saddle numbness, or bladder/bowel dysfunction.

learning_objectives: Differentiate inflammatory back pain from mechanical back pain.

teaching.one_liner: Chronic inflammatory back pain in a young male that improves with exercise and worsens with rest.
red_flags: New leg weakness, saddle numbness, or bladder/bowel dysfunction (possible cauda equina syndrome)

must_ask.say: Is the pain worse after rest and better once you move or exercise?
How long are you stiff after waking up in the morning?

must_ask.objective: Night pain and alternating buttock pain
must_ask.say: Does the pain wake you at night, or move from one buttock to the other?
Have you had a painful red eye, psoriasis, persistent diarrhoea, or bowel symptoms?
Does anyone in your family have similar back problems, psoriasis, or inflammatory bowel disease, and how is this affecting your daily activity?

history.answer: I've had this persistent lower back pain for about six months now, and it's always at its worst and stiffest first thing in the morning.
It's located deep in my lower back and upper buttocks, and sometimes it alternates from one side to the other. It doesn't shoot down past my knees.
It started gradually about six months ago without any sudden trauma or fall. I initially thought I had strained a muscle while lifting weights.
It feels like a deep, persistent ache with severe stiffness. It's around a 6 out of 10 when I wake up, but eases to a 2 or 3 later in the day.
Sitting still or staying in bed makes the stiffness much worse, whereas moving around, working out, or playing sports significantly relieves it. Coughing doesn't aggravate it.
Resting doesn't relieve it at all. In fact, the deep ache often wakes me up during the second half of the night, forcing me to get out of bed and walk around.
When I get out of bed in the morning, my lower back feels completely locked up, and that stiffness lasts for well over an hour before loosening up.
Yes, the deep ache in my buttocks frequently switches back and forth between the left and right sides.
No, I don't have any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my legs or feet.
No issues at all. My bowel and bladder control are completely normal, and I have no numbness around my groin or buttocks.
No, walking doesn't make my legs heavy or numb. In fact, walking helps loosen my back, and I don't need to bend forward to find relief.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss.
No, I have never had cancer or any malignant tumors.
No recent infections, no spinal procedures or injections, no diabetes, and I've never used intravenous drugs.
No, I have never taken steroid medications, and I don't have osteoporosis or any history of fractures.
No abdominal pain, no pulsing sensation in my belly, and no urinary problems or blood in my urine.
No, my eyes haven't been red or painful, and my vision has been completely normal.
I haven't had swollen knees, but a few months ago I had noticeable tenderness and pain in my left heel where the tendon attaches.
No skin rashes, no scaly patches like psoriasis, and my bowel habits are regular with no chronic diarrhea.
I've been taking over-the-counter ibuprofen whenever the stiffness gets bad, and it provides great relief, though the pain returns the next morning.
I assumed I pulled a back muscle while doing deadlifts or squats at the gym, but it has lasted way too long for a simple strain.
I'm worried that I might have a slipped disc or some permanent spinal damage that will keep me from staying active.
I was hoping to get an MRI today so we can see exactly what is wrong with my spine.
The morning stiffness makes getting out of bed and starting my day really sluggish, but once I get moving and exercise, I can manage my work.
None. I don't have any chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and I've never been hospitalized.
Just ibuprofen as needed, usually 400 to 600 milligrams when the stiffness is bad. No other medications or supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two beers on the weekend with friends.
I work as a software developer sitting at a desk during the week, and I live with a roommate in an apartment.
My paternal uncle had severe chronic back stiffness starting in his twenties and was diagnosed with some kind of spinal arthritis.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6 C, SpO2 99% on room air.

Decreased lumbar forward flexion with a positive Schober test (under 5 cm expansion); marked tenderness on direct palpation of bilateral sacroiliac joints; negative bilateral straight-leg raise tests without vertebral midline tenderness.
Tenderness upon palpation at the left Achilles tendon insertion site without warmth or swelling; no active synovitis, effusion, or erythema in the peripheral joints.
Muscle strength is 5/5 across all lower extremity muscle groups including hip flexors, quadriceps, tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, and gastrocnemius bilaterally.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation throughout bilateral lower extremity dermatomes (L2 to S1) and preserved perineal sensation.
Patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric; bilateral plantar responses are flexor.
No conjunctival injection, ciliary flush, or photophobia; pupils are equal, round, and normally reactive to light.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, specifically no early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation, rubs, or gallops.
Clear vesicular breath sounds bilaterally with normal respiratory excursion and no adventitious sounds.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, with no palpable pulsatile abdominal aortic mass or organomegaly.
No costovertebral angle tenderness to percussion on either side.
No erythematous scaly plaques, psoriatic lesions, or nail pitting on skin examination.
